problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.statement:
You are climbing a staircase. It takes `n` steps to reach the top.

Each time you can either climb `1` or `2` steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?

parameterDefinitions.name: n
parameterDefinitions.description: Number of steps to the top

examples.explanation: There are two ways: (1 step + 1 step) or (2 steps).
Only one way to climb 1 step.

commonMistakes: Using raw recursion without memoization leading to O(2^N) time limit exceeded.
Off-by-one indexing on base cases.
hints: To reach step n, you must arrive from either step n - 1 or step n - 2.
dp[n] = dp[n - 1] + dp[n - 2], which is the Fibonacci sequence.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `cost` where `cost[i]` is the cost of `i-th` step on a staircase. Once you pay the cost, you can either climb one or two steps.

You can either start from the step with index `0`, or the step with index `1`.

Return the minimum cost to reach the top of the floor.

parameterDefinitions.name: cost
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of costs for each step

examples.explanation: Start at index 1, pay 15 and climb 2 steps to reach the top.
Take path stepping only on 1s: index 0 -> 2 -> 4 -> 6 -> 7 -> 9 -> top, total cost 6.
All steps cost 0, minimum cost is 0.
Start at index 0 (pay 10) or index 1 (pay 20). Min is 10.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that you can start at either index 0 or index 1.
Reaching step n - 1 instead of top of the floor at index n.
hints: Let dp[i] be the minimum cost to reach step i.
dp[i] = min(dp[i - 1] + cost[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + cost[i - 2]).
Notice dp[i] only depends on the previous two values, so O(1) space is sufficient.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification

problems.title: House Robber
problems.statement:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed, the only constraint stopping you from robbing each of them is that adjacent houses have security systems connected and it will automatically contact the police if two adjacent houses were broken into on the same night.

Given an integer array `nums` representing the amount of money of each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

parameterDefinitions.name: nums
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of money in each house

examples.explanation: Rob house 1 (money = 1) and then rob house 3 (money = 3). Total = 1 + 3 = 4.
Rob house 1 (2), house 3 (9), house 5 (1). Total = 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.
Single house with 0 money.
Rob house 0 (2) and house 3 (2). Total = 4.

commonMistakes: Assuming robbing alternating odd or even houses always gives the optimal sum (e.g. [2, 1, 1, 2] skips two in the middle).
hints: At each house, you have two choices: rob it (which means you couldn't have robbed house i - 1), or skip it.
dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + nums[i]).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=80 for complexity verification

problems.title: House Robber II
problems.statement:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed. All houses at this place are arranged in a circle. That means the first house is the neighbor of the last one.

Meanwhile, adjacent houses have a security system connected, and it will automatically contact the police if two adjacent houses were broken into on the same night.

Given an integer array `nums` representing the amount of money of each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

parameterDefinitions.name: nums
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of money in circular houses

examples.explanation: You cannot rob house 1 (2) and house 3 (2) because they are adjacent in a circle.
Rob house 1 (1) and house 3 (3), total 4.
Max money is house 3 alone.
Only one house, rob it directly.

commonMistakes: Failing to handle nums.length === 1 separately.
Robbing both index 0 and index n - 1.
hints: Since house 0 and house n - 1 are adjacent, you cannot rob both.
Break into two independent linear subproblems: rob(0 ... n - 2) and rob(1 ... n - 1).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=60 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification

problems.title: Delete and Earn
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `nums`. You want to maximize the number of points you get by performing the following operation any number of times:

Pick any `nums[i]` and delete it to earn `nums[i]` points. Afterwards, you must delete every element equal to `nums[i] - 1` and every element equal to `nums[i] + 1`.

Return the maximum number of points you can earn.

examples.explanation: Delete 4 to earn 4 points (3 is deleted). Then delete 2 to earn 2 points. Total 6.
Delete 3 to earn 3*3 = 9 points (deleting all 2s and 4s). Total 9.
Earn 1 point directly.
Delete 1s (3), 5s (15), total 18 points.

commonMistakes: Not noticing that picking a number lets you take all instances of that number without additional penalty.
Missing the mapping to House Robber.
hints: If you decide to take value x, you can take ALL copies of x for a total of x * count[x].
Taking x prohibits taking x - 1 and x + 1. This is exactly House Robber on the value frequency array!

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=200 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification

problems.title: Decode Ways
problems.statement:
A message containing letters from A-Z can be encoded into numbers using the following mapping:
'A' -> "1", 'B' -> "2", ... 'Z' -> "26"

To decode an encoded message, all the digits must be grouped then mapped back into letters using the reverse of the mapping above (there may be multiple ways).

For example, "11106" can be mapped into "AAJF" with the grouping (1 1 10 6) or "KJF" with the grouping (11 10 6). Note that the grouping (1 11 06) is invalid because "06" cannot be mapped into 'F' since "6" is different from "06".

Given a string `s` containing only digits, return the number of ways to decode it.
constraints: s contains only digits and may contain leading zero(s).

examples.explanation: "12" could be decoded as "AB" (1 2) or "L" (12).
"226" could be decoded as "BZ" (2 26), "VF" (22 6), or "BBF" (2 2 6).
"06" cannot be mapped to 'F' because of the leading zero.
"10" maps uniquely to "J".

commonMistakes: Failing to handle '0' characters (e.g. '06' -> 0, '10' -> 1, '30' -> 0).
Index alignment when reading single digit vs two digits.
hints: A single digit is valid if it is between '1' and '9'.
A two-digit substring is valid if it is between '10' and '26'.
If s[i] is '0', it cannot form a single digit character; it must pair with s[i-1].

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=16 for complexity verification

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `coins` representing coins of different denominations and an integer `amount` representing a total amount of money.

Return the fewest number of coins that you need to make up that amount. If that amount of money cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return `-1`.

You may assume that you have an infinite number of each kind of coin.

examples.explanation: Amount 3 cannot be made with only 2-cent coins.
0 coins needed to make 0 amount.

commonMistakes: Using a greedy approach (taking the largest coin first doesn't work, e.g. coins [1, 3, 4] for amount 6: greedy gives 4+1+1=3, optimal is 3+3=2).
hints: Greedy fails on canonical counterexamples like coins=[1,3,4] with amount=6.
Bottom-up DP: dp[i] = min(dp[i - c] + 1) for each coin c <= i.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=6 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=4 for complexity verification

problems.title: Coin Change II
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `coins` representing coins of different denominations and an integer `amount` representing a total amount of money.

Return the number of combinations that make up that amount. If that amount of money cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return `0`.

You may assume that you have an infinite number of each kind of coin.

The answer is guaranteed to fit into a signed 32-bit integer.
constraints: All values of coins are unique

examples.explanation: Amount 3 cannot be made with 2-cent coins.
Only one way: 10.
Only one combination (choose no coins) to make 0.

commonMistakes: Looping over amount in outer loop and coins in inner loop (this counts permutations instead of combinations).
hints: Order matters! To count combinations (not permutations), iterate through coins in the OUTER loop and amount in the INNER loop.
dp[i] represents the number of ways to form amount i using coins processed so far.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Perfect Squares
problems.statement:
Given an integer `n`, return the least number of perfect square numbers that sum to `n`.

A perfect square is an integer that is the square of an integer; in other words, it is the product of some integer with itself. For example, 1, 4, 9, and 16 are perfect squares while 3 and 11 are not.

examples.explanation: 13 = 4 + 9 (2 squares).
16 is itself a perfect square.

commonMistakes: Trying greedy by always subtracting the largest possible square (fails e.g. 12: 9+1+1+1 = 4, but 4+4+4 = 3).
hints: Lagrange's Four-Square Theorem proves the answer is always at most 4.
Use dynamic programming: dp[i] = min(dp[i - j*j] + 1) for all j*j <= i.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Word Break
problems.statement:
Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.

Note that the same word in the dictionary may be reused multiple times in the segmentation.
constraints: s and wordDict[i] consist of only lowercase English letters.
All the strings of wordDict are unique.

examples.explanation: Return true because "leetcode" can be segmented as "leet code".
Return true because "applepenapple" can be segmented as "apple pen apple".
No valid segmentation exists.
"a" is not in wordDict.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N^2 * L) where L is max word length
commonMistakes: Naive recursion without memoization leading to exponential O(2^N) time.
Re-checking long substring slices when max dictionary word length is small.
hints: Let dp[i] be true if s[0...i-1] can be segmented.
dp[i] = true if there exists some j < i such that dp[j] is true and s[j...i-1] is in wordDict.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=15 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=15 for complexity verification

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if you can partition the array into two subsets such that the sum of the elements in both subsets is equal or `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: The array can be partitioned as [1, 5, 5] and [11].
The array cannot be partitioned into equal sum subsets.
Both subsets are [2] and [2].
Sum is 8, but no subset sums to 4.

commonMistakes: Iterating forward in the 1D DP table, which accidentally reuses the same element multiple times (unbounded knapsack).
Forgetting that odd sums can never be partitioned.
hints: If total sum is odd, equal partition is impossible.
This reduces to the 0/1 Knapsack problem: can we find a subset with sum equal to sum / 2?
Iterate backwards from target down to num to maintain 0/1 semantics in 1D array.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`.

You want to build an expression out of nums by adding one of the symbols '+' and '-' before each integer in nums and then concatenate all the integers.

For example, if nums = [2, 1], you can add a '+' before 2 and a '-' before 1 and concatenate them to build the expression "+2-1" = 1.

Return the number of different expressions that you can build, which evaluates to `target`.

examples.explanation: Impossible to form 2 with single 1.
Each of the 8 zeros can be either +0 or -0 (2^8 = 256 ways).

commonMistakes: Forgetting that nums can contain 0s which produce 2^k multiplier.
Failing when Math.abs(target) > total sum.
hints: Let P be the subset of numbers with '+' and N be the subset with '-'.
sum(P) - sum(N) = target and sum(P) + sum(N) = total.
Adding gives 2 * sum(P) = target + total => sum(P) = (target + total) / 2.
The problem reduces to subset sum: count subsets summing to (target + total) / 2.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=10 for complexity verification

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

A subsequence is an array that can be derived from another array by deleting some or no elements without changing the order of the remaining elements.

examples.explanation: The longest increasing subsequence is [2, 3, 7, 101], length 4.
One longest increasing subsequence is [0, 1, 2, 3], length 4.
All elements are equal, longest strictly increasing subsequence has length 1.
Increasing subsequence [1,3,6,7,9,10] has length 6.

commonMistakes: Confusing strictly increasing (<) with non-decreasing (<=).
Assuming tails array itself is the final subsequence (tails stores minimal tail elements).
hints: O(N^2) dynamic programming is straightforward: dp[i] = max(dp[j] + 1) for all j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
To achieve O(N log N), maintain array `tails` where tails[k] is the smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1, updating via binary search (Patience Sorting).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=150 for complexity verification

problems.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return the number of longest increasing subsequences.

Notice that the sequence has to be strictly increasing.

examples.explanation: Two longest increasing subsequences of length 4: [1, 3, 4, 7] and [1, 3, 5, 7].
The length of longest increasing subsequence is 1, and there are 5 such subsequences.
Single element has exactly 1 LIS.

commonMistakes: Resetting counts[i] to 1 when lengths[j] + 1 === lengths[i] instead of accumulating counts[j].
Only counting the single longest ending at the last index.
hints: Maintain two DP arrays: lengths[i] storing LIS length ending at i, and counts[i] storing the number of such subsequences.
When lengths[j] + 1 > lengths[i], reset counts[i] = counts[j].
When lengths[j] + 1 == lengths[i], accumulate counts[i] += counts[j].

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=60 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=80 for complexity verification

problems.title: Integer Break
problems.statement:
Given an integer `n`, break it into the sum of `k` positive integers, where `k >= 2`, and maximize the product of those integers.

Return the maximum product you can get.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the constraint k >= 2 (for n = 2 and n = 3, we must break them even though their unbroken value is higher).
hints: By calculus, factor e ≈ 2.718 maximizes product, so factors of 3 (and occasionally 2) yield the maximal product.
Break n into as many 3s as possible. If remainder is 4, use 2 * 2 rather than 3 * 1.

problems.title: Paint House
problems.statement:
There is a row of `n` houses, where each house can be painted one of three colors: red, blue, or green. The cost of painting each house with a certain color is different. You have to paint all the houses such that no two adjacent houses have the same color.

The cost of painting each house with a certain color is represented by an `n x 3` cost matrix `costs`.

For example, `costs[0][0]` is the cost of painting house 0 with color red; `costs[1][2]` is the cost of painting house 1 with color green, and so on.

Return the minimum cost to paint all houses.

parameterDefinitions.name: costs
parameterDefinitions.description: n x 3 matrix of painting costs

examples.explanation: Paint house 0 blue (cost 2), house 1 green (cost 5), house 2 blue (cost 3). Total = 10.
Paint house 0 green with min cost 2.
House 0 red (1) + House 1 green (1) = 2, wait: adjacent colors are red(0) and green(2) which is cost 1 + 1 = 2 or 1 + 2 = 3 depending on indices. Min is 2.
Paint optimal alternating color choices to yield 43.

commonMistakes: Greedily picking the minimum for each house independently, ignoring color collision on future houses.
hints: Let r, b, g be the min cost to paint up to the previous house ending in red, blue, or green.
The new red cost is current red cost + min(previous blue, previous green).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=80 for complexity verification

problems.title: Paint Fence
problems.statement:
You have a fence of `n` posts, each post can be painted with one of the `k` colors. You have to paint all the posts such that no more than two adjacent fence posts have the same color.

Given the two integers `n` and `k`, return the number of ways to paint the fence.
constraints: The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer for n <= 50.

examples.explanation: All 6 valid colorings with colors 0 and 1: 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110.
Only 1 post and 1 color gives 1 way.
Total 42 valid ways.
Every pair of colors is valid for n = 2 posts: 4 * 4 = 16.

commonMistakes: Allowing three consecutive posts of the same color.
Base cases for n = 1 or n = 2.
hints: For post i, it can either have the SAME color as post i-1 or a DIFFERENT color.
same[i] = diff[i-1] (since we cannot have 3 consecutive same colors).
diff[i] = (same[i-1] + diff[i-1]) * (k - 1).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Minimum Cost For Tickets
problems.statement:
You have planned some train traveling one year in advance. The days of the year in which you will travel are given as an integer array `days`. Each day is an integer from 1 to 365.

Train tickets are sold in three different ways:
- a 1-day pass is sold for `costs[0]` dollars,
- a 7-day pass is sold for `costs[1]` dollars, and
- a 30-day pass is sold for `costs[2]` dollars.

The passes allow that many days of consecutive travel.

Return the minimum number of dollars you need to travel every day in the given list of days.

examples.explanation: Buy 7-day pass on day 1 for $7 (covering 1-7). Buy 1-day pass on day 8 for $2. Buy 1-day pass on day 20 for $2. Total 11.
Buy 30-day pass on day 1 for $15 (covers 1-30). Buy 1-day pass on day 31 for $2. Total 17.
Single day trip, buy 1-day pass for $5.
Two separate days, two 1-day passes = $4.

commonMistakes: Incrementing days linearly without checking if the day is an actual travel day.
hints: If day i is not a travel day, dp[i] = dp[i - 1].
If day i is a travel day, dp[i] = min(dp[i - 1] + cost[0], dp[i - 7] + cost[1], dp[i - 30] + cost[2]).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification

problems.title: Triangle
problems.statement:
Given a `triangle` array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom.

For each step, you may move to an adjacent number of the row below. More formally, if you are on index `i` on the current row, you may move to either index `i` or index `i + 1` on the next row.

examples.explanation: Minimum path sum from top to bottom is 2 + 3 + 5 + 1 = 11.
Only one element: -10.

commonMistakes: Top-down approach requiring complex boundary checking instead of bottom-up which converges cleanly to dp[0].
hints: Work bottom-up: starting from the second to last row, each cell's optimal path sum is its value plus min(dp[c], dp[c+1]).
Requires only O(N) auxiliary space using a single 1D row.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=60 for complexity verification

problems.title: Fibonacci Number
problems.statement:
The Fibonacci numbers, commonly denoted `F(n)` form a sequence, called the Fibonacci sequence, such that each number is the sum of the two preceding ones, starting from 0 and 1. That is:
F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1
F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2), for n > 1.

Given `n`, calculate `F(n)`.
commonMistakes: Naive exponential recursion O(2^N) instead of linear dynamic programming.
hints: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) with base cases F(0)=0 and F(1)=1.
Store the last two calculated values for O(1) space.
